en: The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on Śyāma’s Son, translated by the Śramaṇa Shengjian of the Western Qin under imperial decree.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Pilala with twelve hundred and fifty [monks].

The bhikṣus gathered together, along with a multitude of bodhisattvas, kings, ministers, and commoners—incalculable numbers of elders, householders, laymen, and laywomen—all came to the assembly at once.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
“All of you, listen with minds of complete tranquility and concentration!

I recall my past lives when I first sought to attain the path of a bodhisattva. My observance of the precepts was universal and compassionate; my diligence was single-minded; and my wisdom, skillful means, and expedients were beyond description—such that no devas, nāgas, spirits, kings, or common people were able to practice them.”
Having heard what the Buddha said, Ānanda adjusted his robes, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and addressed the Buddha:
“I wish to hear it.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"In the distant past, incalculable eons ago, there was a bodhisattva named Maitrīmati who rescued and delivered all living beings. He constantly practiced the four immeasurable minds, saving the world from peril and distress, and compassionately nurturing those in suffering."
Thereupon, while residing in the Tuṣita Heaven, he instructed the devas.

Constantly, during each of the three periods of day and night, he entered samādhi with a concentrated mind to contemplate the three realms and to illuminate and observe the paths of good and evil among the people throughout the ten directions of the world.

Filially supporting one's parents, reverently serving the Triple Gem, attending to teachers and elders, and cultivating all manner of meritorious virtues—all these are clearly perceived, and the five realms of existence are distinctly revealed.

At that time, there was an elder in the kingdom of Kāśī who was childless; both his eyes were blind, yet he and his wife desired to enter the mountains to seek unsurpassed wisdom, cultivating pure resolve and delighting in solitude.
The Bodhisattva thought to himself:

"This person has resolved to study the wondrous Way, yet his two eyes are blind and he can see nothing. If he enters the mountains, he may fall into a ravine or pit, or encounter venomous insects that will bring him harm. When my life comes to an end, I shall become his son, providing for my parents until the end of their years."
He was immediately reborn into the home of blind parents as their son.

His parents loved him with great joy and affection; though they had originally resolved to set their minds on the Way and enter the mountains, because of the birth of this son, they became attached to the world.
When the son was seven years old, he was given the name Śyāma. Śyāma was profoundly filial, compassionate, and benevolent, practicing the ten wholesome deeds:

refraining from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, deceit, drinking intoxicants, false speech, and envy; he followed the Way without doubt and practiced with diligence day and night. He served his parents as one serves the heavens; his speech was always accompanied by a smile so as not to offend others' feelings, and his conduct accorded with the Dharma, never being frivolous or deviant. Thereupon, his parents were filled with great joy, and their sorrows vanished.
When Śyāma was over ten years old, he knelt upright and addressed his parents, saying:
"I have originally resolved upon the Great Intention to enter the deep mountains to seek the supreme Way of empty stillness; how could I abandon my fundamental vow for the sake of a son?"

Human life in this world is subject to the hundredfold changes of impermanence; life is not of stone or metal, and its end arrives without fixed date. It would be fitting to fulfill our original intention and honor our prior resolve: let us follow our parents together into the mountains, providing for their needs with due care and never missing the proper seasons.
The parents replied to Śyāma, "Your filial piety is known to Heaven; do not violate your original vow, and you may enter the mountains immediately.
Śyāma then took all the wealth and treasures in the household and gave them in great alms to the poor, after which he entered the mountains together with his parents.
"Śāṇa went into the mountains and constructed a hut from firewood and grass; he prepared beds and mats that were neither cold nor hot, always providing the perfect comfort.
After one year in the mountains, various fruits became abundant and their taste was sweet and delicious; springs gushed forth, clear and cool;
lotuses of five colors bloomed in the ponds with brilliant luster; sandalwood blended with various fragrances, and the trees flourished, their scent twice as strong as usual."
Birds constantly gathered there, including all manner of wondrous and exotic species, who together produced the sounds of various kinds of music to entertain their parents;
even lions, bears, cubs, tigers, wolves, and venomous insects faced one another with hearts of compassion, without harming each other.
Eating grass and drinking water, they were no longer afraid; deer and various birds all came to stay near him, their calls blending with Śāṇa’s voice in a harmonious and joyful chorus.

Śyāma was supremely filial and compassionate; when he stepped upon the ground, he constantly feared it might suffer pain. Thus, devas, spirits, humans, and ghosts all came to protect these three practitioners of the Way.
As for these three practitioners of the Way, they focused their minds with single-minded concentration, free once more from all sorrow and anxiety.
"Śyāma constantly gathered a hundred kinds of fruits with his parents to feed them, and the spring water never failed.

At that time, when his parents were thirsty and wished to drink, Śyāma, wearing a deer-skin garment, took a pitcher and went to fetch water; the deer and various birds also went there to drink, and none feared or troubled one another."
At that time, the King of Kāśī entered the mountains to hunt. Seeing a herd of deer by the water's edge, the king drew his bow and shot at them.
By mistake, the arrow struck Śyāma, hitting him squarely in the chest.
Once struck by the poisoned arrow, his entire body was in agony, and he cried out loudly, "Who has shot three practitioners of the Way with a single arrow?
Hearing the voice of a man, the king immediately dismounted and went before Śyāma. Śyāma said to the king:

"Elephants die because of their tusks; rhinoceroses die because of their horns; peacocks die because of their feathers; and deer die because of their hides and flesh. I have no tusks, no horns, no feathers, and no hide or flesh that can be eaten. What crime have I committed that I am now being shot and killed so pointlessly?"
The king asked Śyāma, "Who are you?
You are dressed in deer skin and are no different from the beasts."
Śyāma said:

"I am a man from within this kingdom who has come with my blind parents for more than twenty years to study the Way. Never before have I been harmed by tigers, wolves, or venomous insects; yet now I have been shot and killed by Your Majesty."

"At that moment, a great tempest arose, blowing down and breaking the trees; hundreds of birds wailed in sorrow, and the lions, bears, brown bears, and various wild beasts all let out great roars, shaking the entire mountain.
The sun lost its brilliance, the flowing springs ran dry, the myriad flowers withered and died, and thunder and lightning shook the earth."
At that time, the blind parents suddenly rose in alarm and said, "What strange occurrence is this?
Śyāma has been gone for a long time fetching water and has not yet returned; could it be that he has been harmed by venomous insects?"
"The birds and beasts cry out in grief; their clamorous calls are unlike those of ordinary times. Winds rise from the four directions and the trees are broken and snapped;
there must be some calamitous anomaly. At that time, the king was terrified and deeply reproached himself:

"Originally, I shot at a herd of deer and mistakenly struck this man. To shoot and kill a practitioner of the Way is a most grievous sin. Because I was greedy for a small amount of meat, I have incurred this disaster. I pray that you will accept these rare treasures to save my son's life."

Then the king stepped forward, intending to pull out the arrow; however, the arrow was so deeply embedded that it could not be extracted. Hundreds of birds and beasts gathered from all sides like clouds, all crying out loudly, making the entire mountain shake.
The king became even more terrified, his limbs trembling all over. Śyāma said to the king, "This is not the fault of the King!

It is caused by the karmic retribution of my own past offenses. I do not begrudge my body; I only think of my blind parents. They are already advanced in years and both eyes are blind; if I am gone one day, they will also perish, having no one to look after them. For this reason, I am merely distressed."
At that moment, all the devas, nāgas, and spirits were moved with solemn awe.
The King spoke again:
"I would rather enter the midst of hell myself and undergo this retribution than allow Śyāma’s life to be restored."
Kneeling long on his knees toward Śyāma, he repented and spoke these words:

"If you, my son, should ultimately pass away, I shall not return to the kingdom, but will instead remain in the mountains to provide for your blind parents just as when you were here. Do not be anxious; the devas, nāgas, and spirits shall all bear witness that I do not violate this vow."
When Śyāma heard the king’s vow, he said:

"Though I am struck by a poisoned arrow, my heart is joyful and my mind is glad; even in death I have no regret. Entrust my parents to the King for their support; by doing so, the King’s transgressions shall be extinguished and he shall obtain immeasurable merit."
The King said, "You must tell me where my parents are; while my son has not yet died, I wish to know.
Śyāma immediately pointed them out.
"Proceed along this path; not far from here you will see a thatched hut where my parents reside.

Your Majesty, proceed slowly so as not to startle or terrify them. With skillful means, explain my intentions to them: 'Your Majesty, please inform my parents on my behalf that impermanence has now arrived and I am about to depart for the next world.'"

I do not begrudge my life; rather, I am distressed because my blind parents are already advanced in years and both have lost their sight. Should I suddenly be gone, they would have no one to rely upon, and for this reason I torment myself with such grief.

My death is brought about by my own past karmic offenses; there is no way to escape it. Now I repent for all the various evils I have committed since having taken on a body throughout incalculable kalpas. May these sins be extinguished here and now. I pray that I may meet with my parents life after life, never to be separated from them, and that they may enjoy full longevity without any sorrow or affliction. May devas, nāgas, and spirits constantly follow and protect us, so that calamities are eliminated and our desires are fulfilled according to our wishes, occurring spontaneously and without effort.
The king took several attendants and went to his parents’ abode; after the king had departed, Śyāma suddenly died.
Hundreds of birds and beasts gathered from all directions like clouds, all wailing loudly as they circled Śyāma’s corpse, licking the blood upon his chest.
Hearing this sound, the blind parents became even more terrified and stood there wandering restlessly.
As the king traveled swiftly, he brushed against the grasses and trees, creating a rustling noise;
the parents cried out in alarm, "Who is this person?"
"This is not the conduct of my son.
The king said, "I am the King of Kāśī.
Hearing that a blind man was practicing the Way in the mountains, I have come to make offerings to him."
The blind parents said:
"Your Majesty has condescended to come and comfort us, traveling so far to this humble wilderness; we pray that you have not been overexhausted and that your person remains in good health."
Are the palace ladies, the crown prince, and the officials all well?
Are the winds and rains harmonious, and are the five grains abundant?
Do the people of neighboring states not harm one another?
The king replied to the practitioner,
"I have been graced by your venerable kindness and am always at peace.
He then further inquired after the welfare of his blind parents:
"In this mountain, you have undergone great toil and hardship; amidst these trees, it must be very difficult to find rest. Are you at peace?

The blind parents replied, "By the grace of Your Majesty, we are always at peace. We have a filial son named Śyāma, who constantly gathers fruits, melons, and spring water so that we lack for nothing."
"I have a grass mat; Your Majesty may sit upon it, and there are fruits and melons to eat.
Śāṇa has gone to fetch water and will return shortly.
Upon hearing the words of the blind parents, the king was once again deeply moved by grief and spoke these words through his tears:
"My transgression is indeed grave. While entering the mountains to hunt, I saw a herd of deer by the water's edge from afar; drawing my bow, I shot at them, but by mistake my arrow struck Śyama.
The ascetic’s son Śyama has already been pierced by the poisoned arrow, and his pain is most excruciating; this is why I have come here in person to speak to the ascetic."
Upon hearing this, the parents threw themselves to the ground, like a great mountain collapsing and the earth trembling violently. Wailing and looking toward heaven, they lamented, saying:
"Our son Śyāma was the most filial in all the world; none could surpass him. He walked upon the earth ever fearing he might cause it pain; for what crime has he been shot and killed?"
Just now, a great wind suddenly arose, blowing down and breaking the trees; the hundred birds wailed in sorrow, all crying out so loudly that it shook the entire mountain.

I have lived in these mountains for over twenty years, yet never before have there been such calamitous portents. Now my son Śyāma has gone to fetch water and does not return; I fear there must be some cause for this, and thus all the deities are startled, trembling with solemn awe.
The mother then wept and wailed, refusing to stop; the father said, "Cease for now!
In this world of men, who is there that does not die?"
"Impermanence has arrived; it cannot be warded off.
He then asked the king, "Where did you shoot Śyāma? Is he dead or alive now?"
The king related Śyāma’s words to his parents; hearing these words from the king, the blind parents were again overcome with profound grief, saying:
"If we suddenly lose our son, we both shall surely die."
"Great King!
Now lead us two to our son’s corpse.

The king immediately led the blind parents to the corpse; the father embraced his head and the mother embraced both his feet, placing them upon her knees. Each used both hands to feel for Śyāma’s arrow, looking up to heaven and crying out:
"The various devas, nāgas, mountain spirits, and tree spirits know that my son, Śyāma, was the most filial in the world; this is known to all these devas, nāgas, and spirits."
"I am already old and my eyes can no longer see; it would be no regret for me to die in place of my son so that Śyāma may live.
Thereupon, the parents both made a solemn vow together:
"If Śyāma’s supreme filial piety is known to Heaven and Earth, then the arrow shall be pulled out, the poisonous pain shall be removed, and Śyāma shall return to life."

Thereupon, the throne of the second Lord of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven trembled. Seeing with his own eyes these two blind practitioners of the Way embracing their son and wailing, he heard that Śakra, Brahmā, and the Four Heavenly Kings were coming from the fourth Tuṣita Heaven. In the time it takes a man to bend and stretch his arm, they arrived and stood before Śyāma; they poured divine and wondrous medicine into Śyāma’s mouth. As the medicine entered his mouth, the arrow was extracted and the poison expelled, and he was restored to life as he had been before.

When the parents heard that Śyāma had returned to life after death, both their eyes opened; birds and beasts all uttered sounds of great joy; the wind ceased and the clouds dispersed so that the sun shone with renewed brilliance; flowing springs gushed forth, clear and cool; lotuses of five colors bloomed in the ponds with radiant purity; and the fragrance of various sandalwoods and trees was twice as intense as usual.

At that time, the king was so overcome with joy that he could not contain himself. He paid homage to Śakra, the Lord of Devas, and then returned his salutations to his parents and to his son, Śyāma, saying:

"I wish to offer all the wealth and treasures of this entire kingdom to these practitioners of the Way, so that we may provide for one another and cause my transgressions to be extinguished forever without remainder."
Śyāma said to the king:

"If you wish to cultivate merit, Your Majesty should simply return to your kingdom and comfort your people, ensuring they uphold the precepts. Do not hunt or kill the innocent wantonly; for your body will find no peace, and when your life ends, you shall enter the hells."
When people dwell in this world, affection and love are but temporary; separation lasts long and one cannot remain forever together.

Your Majesty, having possessed merit in past lives, you have now become king; do not be arrogant in your sovereignty. Because of such sovereignty, you may commit immeasurable evils, which will lead you later into the evil realms—what benefit would there be in regretting it then?
The King replied, "As you have instructed.

The King's hunters, seeing that Śyāma had died, obtained the medicine of the devas so that he died and was reborn; his parents' eyes were opened by such a divine transformation. They all received the five precepts and practiced the ten wholesome deeds; upon death, they attained birth in the heavens and did not enter the evil realms.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Among those gathered here, he who was Śyāma in his past lives is my own self;
the blind father is King Śuddhodana."
The blind mother was the current Queen Māyā;
the King of the Kāśī country was Ānanda;
and Śakra, Lord of the Devas, was Maitreya Buddha.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"In my previous lives, as a son I was benevolent and filial; as a ruler I was compassionate and nurturing; as a subject I was reverent and respectful. Thus, I have attained for myself the status of the Honored One of the Three Realms."
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, all the bodhisattvas, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās were filled with joy; they paid their respects and departed.
The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on the Son Śyāma.
